techniques.name: Algorithm Review Boards
techniques.description: An algorithm review board, also called an AI ethics board or AI review board, is a standing group from different disciplines that examines proposed AI systems or AI research projects before they proceed. It differs from an Institutional Review Board (IRB), which protects the human subjects of research, because it also weighs harms to the people a system will affect and to society. Many boards first sort projects by risk, and for higher-risk work the project team submits a written account of the system's purpose, data, foreseeable harms and planned mitigations, which members with technical, legal, ethical and domain backgrounds question and iterate on with the team. Where it has the power to decide, the board approves, approves with conditions such as a monitoring plan or a re-review date, or rejects; where it only advises, it recommends one of these. It keeps a dated record of its decision, reasons and conditions that later reviews and audits can check against what was built, and some organisations share that record with an oversight body or publish it.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital group's algorithm review board examines a sepsis early-warning model before a ward pilot. It approves the pilot on condition of a monitoring plan for alert rates and missed cases, names who may switch the model off, and sets a re-review once six months of local performance data are in, before any wider roll-out.

A bank's board reviews a proposed credit-limit model before launch. It asks the team for its disparate-impact analysis by protected group and for evidence that applicants can contest a decision, and withholds approval until both are supplied, so the decision to deploy rests with a body outside the development team.

A university AI research programme releases grant funding only after each project has passed an ethics and society review, in which researchers state the risks their work poses to society and to particular groups, commit to mitigations, and revise them with an interdisciplinary faculty panel.

A government department publishes the board's decision record for a benefits-triage tool, giving the reasons for approval, the conditions attached and the re-review date, so that its oversight committee and the public can see what was examined, by whom and when, and check later that the conditions were met.

limitations.description: Review adds time and cost to every project that goes through it, and organisations under commercial pressure may route work around the board or narrow its remit, so the board's coverage, not just its existence, needs to be shown.

Its judgements are only as good as its membership. A board without the relevant technical, domain or community expertise will miss harms that fall outside what its members know, and a board drawn mainly from inside the team's own reporting line is open to group-think.

Independence is hard to keep inside an organisation. Practitioners report tension between profit and the cost of responsible-AI review, and a board can come under pressure to approve projects that leadership has already committed to, which weakens it most where review matters most.

Without authority to stop or delay a project, and a way to check that its conditions are met, a board's recommendations can be ignored. Evidence from a board is strong only when its decision record shows what it could block and what happened to its conditions.

There is no agreed measure of whether a board works, and review can become box-ticking. A record that a project was reviewed shows that a process ran, not that the review was substantive or that its concerns were addressed.

resources.title: Looking before we leap: Expanding ethical review processes for AI and data science research
resources.abstract: Expanding ethical review processes for AI and data science research

resources.title: How to design an AI ethics board
resources.abstract: The development and deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) systems poses significant risks to society. To reduce these risks to an acceptable level, AI companies need an effective risk management process and sound risk governance. In this paper, we explore a particular way in which AI companies can improve their risk governance: by setting up an AI ethics board. We identify five key design choices: (1) What responsibilities should the board have? (2) What should its legal structure be? (3) Who should sit on the board? (4) How should it make decisions? (5) And what resources does it need? We break each of these questions down into more specific sub-questions, list options, and discuss how different design choices affect the board’s ability to reduce societal risks from AI. Several failures have shown that designing an AI ethics board can be challenging. This paper provides a toolbox that can help AI companies to overcome these challenges.

resources.title: Designing Artificial Intelligence Review Boards: Creating Risk Metrics for Review of AI
resources.abstract: Discussions of the need for a review committee dedicated to ethical oversight of artificial intelligence (AI) research have not yet advanced to organization design discussions. What are the essential components for an AI research review board? Based upon precedent for composition and conduct of high-technology review boards, one essential component is a risk-adjusted review mechanism that assists review boards in the categorization of research needing review. In this paper, risk assessment tools are developed based upon lessons learned from other review boards, such as Institutional Biosafety Committees.

resources.title: Ethics and society review: Ethics reflection as a precondition to research funding
resources.abstract: Researchers in areas as diverse as computer science and political science must increasingly navigate the possible risks of their research to society. However, the history of medical experiments on vulnerable individuals influenced many research ethics reviews to focus exclusively on risks to human subjects rather than risks to human society. We describe an Ethics and Society Review board (ESR), which fills this moral gap by facilitating ethical and societal reflection as a requirement to access grant funding: Researchers cannot receive grant funding from participating programs until the researchers complete the ESR process for their proposal. Researchers author an initial statement describing their proposed research’s risks to society, subgroups within society, and globally and commit to mitigation strategies for these risks. An interdisciplinary faculty panel iterates with the researchers to refine these risks and mitigation strategies. We describe a mixed-method evaluation of the ESR over 1 y, in partnership with an artificial intelligence grant program run by Stanford HAI. Surveys and interviews of researchers who interacted with the ESR found 100% (95% CI: 87 to 100%) were willing to continue submitting future projects to the ESR, and 58% (95% CI: 37 to 77%) felt that it had influenced the design of their research project. The ESR panel most commonly identified issues of harms to minority groups, inclusion of diverse stakeholders in the research plan, dual use, and representation in datasets. These principles, paired with possible mitigation strategies, offer scaffolding for future research designs.

resources.title: ESR Process & Toolkit — Stanford Ethics & Society Review
resources.abstract: The Ethics and Society Review is improving ethical reflection in research by bringing together a panel of ethics experts to help researchers identify and mitigate negative ethical or societal aspects of their research and elevate the positive.

resources.title: Investigating Algorithm Review Boards for Organizational Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance
resources.abstract: Organizations are increasingly developing and utilizing artificial intelligence (AI) tools. Responsible AI (RAI) governance approaches including algorithm review board (ARBs) have emerged as important mechanisms to address potential AI risks and harms. We interviewed 17 technical contributors at a variety of organizations about their experiences with internal RAI governance. We summarized the first detailed findings on ARBs in practice, including their membership, scope, and measures of success. We confirmed known ARBs in finance sectors and revealed extensive use of ARBs in health sectors. Our findings suggest that Institutional Review Boards alone are insufficient for algorithm governance and that ARBs are used in tandem with other RAI approaches. Integration with existing processes and leadership buy-in were considered critical to the success of internal RAI governance. Financial tensions between profit and the cost of RAI were a major concern for many participants. Future work should explore measurements of success for ARBs and expand analysis of ARBs to other industries leading in AI implementation.

resources.title: A framework for the oversight and local deployment of safe and high-quality prediction models
resources.abstract: Artificial intelligence/machine learning models are being rapidly developed and used in clinical practice. However, many models are deployed without a clear understanding of clinical or operational impact and frequently lack monitoring plans that can detect potential safety signals. There is a lack of consensus in establishing governance to deploy, pilot, and monitor algorithms within operational healthcare delivery workflows. Here, we describe a governance framework that combines current regulatory best practices and lifecycle management of predictive models being used for clinical care. Since January 2021, we have successfully added models to our governance portfolio and are currently managing 52 models.

sample_claims.text: Every high-risk AI system was reviewed and approved by the organisation's algorithm review board before operational use, and the board could have blocked deployment
The conditions the review board attached to the credit-limit model's approval, including a disparate-impact analysis by protected group and a re-review date, were met before and after launch
The clinical decision-support model was deployed under a monitoring plan and re-review schedule set by a multidisciplinary review board independent of the development team
The diagnostic AI system's development and deployment decisions are traceable to dated board decision records that state the risks assessed, the reasons for approval and the conditions attached
The review board's decision record for the risk assessment tool, with its reasons and conditions, is available to the oversight body and the public

techniques.name: Red Teaming
techniques.description: Red teaming is a structured exercise in which a team deliberately tries to make an AI system fail, so that weaknesses are found before real users or attackers find them. The organisers set the scope and the harms of concern, recruit people with a mix of skills (for example security testers, domain specialists and members of affected groups), and give them a way to log each attempt and judge whether it worked. Participants try manipulative prompts, awkward edge cases and requests designed to draw out harmful, insecure or discriminatory responses, combining many approaches where a test for one known weakness, such as prompt injection, covers only one. The result is a record of the failures found and how easily each was provoked, which is not a pass or fail verdict. It feeds a risk register (the list of known risks and who owns them) and fixes, and the exercise is repeated when the system changes.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital convenes clinicians, medical students and engineers to stress-test a language model that drafts clinical notes, using real patient cases. Each response that could harm a patient, such as a wrong dosage, is logged and sent to the clinical safety officer to decide on fixes and on how staff may use the tool.

Before launch, a bank's security team and outside testers spend two weeks trying to make its customer-service assistant leak client data or obey instructions hidden in uploaded documents. Each successful attack is written up with the steps to reproduce it and ranked by how easily it was exploited, so engineers can fix the worst first.

A local authority asks advice charities and its own caseworkers to probe a chatbot that explains benefit entitlements. They look for answers that differ or discourage claims depending on a person's nationality, disability or first language, and record each case with the prompt that provoked it, for the authority to fix or justify.

An insurer's AI governance committee requires a red-team report before any customer-facing model goes live. Findings are entered in the risk register with an owner and a due date, and the committee signs off only when each high-severity item is fixed or formally accepted.

limitations.description: Needs people who understand both the system and how attackers work, and some harms need domain specialists to judge, for example whether chemical instructions are accurate. Exercises are therefore costly and hard to scale across many systems.

Finds only what the team thinks to try. In Anthropic's original exercise with 324 crowd workers, no attacks targeted code generation although the models had been trained partly on code, so coverage depends on who is recruited and how they are briefed.

Results describe one model version, configuration and set of safeguards at one moment. After an update or a prompt change, fixed failures can return and new ones appear, so the exercise has to be repeated, which adds cost each time.

Tester-written attacks may differ from real misuse, and there is no agreed measure of success. In Anthropic's study, participants' own ratings and an automated harm score correlated only imperfectly, and a minority of participants produced most attacks, so exercises are hard to compare.

A report with few findings can be read as proof of safety when it shows only that this team did not find a failure in the time available. Reports should state scope, effort and what was not tried, or they invite false confidence.

resources.title: OWASP GenAI Red Teaming Guide
resources.abstract: Discover the GenAI Red Teaming Guide for comprehensive strategies to identify and mitigate security risks in AI-driven systems through red teaming techniques.

resources.title: PyRIT: The Python Risk Identification Tool for generative AI
resources.abstract: The Python Risk Identification Tool for generative AI (PyRIT) is an open source framework built to empower security professionals and engineers to proactively identify risks in generative AI systems.

resources.title: Red Teaming Language Models to Reduce Harms: Methods, Scaling Behaviors, and Lessons Learned
resources.abstract: We describe our early efforts to red team language models in order to simultaneously discover, measure, and attempt to reduce their potentially harmful outputs. We make three main contributions. First, we investigate scaling behaviors for red teaming across 3 model sizes (2.7B, 13B, and 52B parameters) and 4 model types: a plain language model (LM); an LM prompted to be helpful, honest, and harmless; an LM with rejection sampling; and a model trained to be helpful and harmless using reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). We find that the RLHF models are increasingly difficult to red team as they scale, and we find a flat trend with scale for the other model types. Second, we release our dataset of 38,961 red team attacks for others to analyze and learn from. We provide our own analysis of the data and find a variety of harmful outputs, which range from offensive language to more subtly harmful non-violent unethical outputs. Third, we exhaustively describe our instructions, processes, statistical methodologies, and uncertainty about red teaming. We hope that this transparency accelerates our ability to work together as a community in order to develop shared norms, practices, and technical standards for how to red team language models.

resources.title: Red Teaming LLM Applications - DeepLearning.AI
Red teaming ChatGPT in medicine to yield real-world insights on model behavior
resources.abstract: Red teaming, the practice of adversarially exposing unexpected or undesired model behaviors, is critical towards improving equity and accuracy of large language models, but non-model creator-affiliated red teaming is scant in healthcare. We convened teams of clinicians, medical and engineering students, and technical professionals (80 participants total) to stress-test models with real-world clinical cases and categorize inappropriate responses along axes of safety, privacy, hallucinations/accuracy, and bias. Six medically-trained reviewers re-analyzed prompt-response pairs and added qualitative annotations. Of 376 unique prompts (1504 responses), 20.1% were inappropriate (GPT-3.5: 25.8%; GPT-4.0: 16%; GPT-4.0 with Internet: 17.8%). Subsequently, we show the utility of our benchmark by testing GPT-4o, a model released after our event (20.4% inappropriate). 21.5% of responses appropriate with GPT-3.5 were inappropriate in updated models. We share insights for constructing red teaming prompts, and present our benchmark for iterative model assessments.

sample_claims.text: A red-team exercise with clinicians and engineers tested the clinical-notes assistant against the hazards in its safety case, and every high-severity failure it found has a recorded fix or an accepted-risk decision.
The customer-service assistant was red-teamed for prompt injection and extraction of client data before launch, and each successful attack was fixed and re-tested.
A red-team exercise that included people from the affected groups probed the benefits assistant for discriminatory answers, and every case found has been triaged and fixed or formally accepted.
Each customer-facing model had a red-team report reviewed by the governance committee before release, and its open findings are logged in the risk register with owners and due dates.
Red-team attacks against the deployed assistant are repeated after every model or prompt change, and newly successful attacks are tracked until they are resolved.

techniques.name: Human-in-the-Loop Safeguards
techniques.description: Human-in-the-loop safeguards hold an AI system's output at a checkpoint until a trained person has reviewed it. Designers set the rules that send a case to review, such as low model confidence (the system's own estimate of how likely it is to be right), a high-stakes outcome or a request to appeal. Some schemes also review a random sample of routine cases to audit the rest. The reviewer approves, changes or rejects the output, and the record of each review shows how often people overrode the system. Review protects only where reviewers keep using independent judgement, so the design also has to guard against over-trust and fatigue.

example_use_cases.description: Implementing mandatory human physician review for any medical AI diagnostic recommendation before treatment decisions are made, especially for complex cases or when the system confidence is below established thresholds, ensuring patient safety through expert oversight.

Requiring human review of automated loan approval decisions when applicants request explanations or appeal rejections, allowing human underwriters to provide clear reasoning and ensure customers understand the decision-making process behind their application outcomes.

A recruitment agency requires a named recruiter to confirm or reverse every automated rejection before it is sent, and logs the decision and the reason. The agency's governance board reviews the override rate each quarter to see whether the screening tool and its reviewers are working as intended.

limitations.description: Review capacity sets a ceiling. As volume rises, cases queue, decisions are delayed and time-sensitive uses become impractical, so the escalation rules must be tuned to what the available trained reviewers can handle.
Reviewers tire and drift. Attention and consistency fall over a long shift or a run of similar cases, so two reviewers, or one reviewer at different times, may decide the same case differently.

Automation bias. People tend to accept a system's recommendation, particularly under time pressure, so review can become a rubber stamp. A very high approval rate with almost no overrides may signal this rather than a good system.

The escalation rules decide what a human ever sees. A confidently wrong output passes without review when only low-confidence cases are escalated, so reviewing a random sample of routine cases is needed to find these errors.

Human review does not reliably improve decisions. A meta-analysis of 106 experiments found human-AI combinations performed worse on average than the better of human or AI alone, with losses in decision-making tasks. The effect of a checkpoint should be tested, not assumed.

resources.title: Improving the Applicability of AI for Psychiatric Applications through Human-in-the-loop Methodologies
resources.abstract: Objectives Machine learning (ML) and natural language processing have great potential to improve efficiency and accuracy in diagnosis, treatment recommendations, predictive interventions, and scarce resource allocation within psychiatry. Researchers often conceptualize such an approach as operating in isolation without much need for human involvement, yet it remains crucial to harness human-in-the-loop practices when developing and implementing such techniques as their absence may be catastrophic. We advocate for building ML-based technologies that collaborate with experts within psychiatry in all stages of implementation and use to increase model performance while simultaneously increasing the practicality, robustness, and reliability of the process. Methods We showcase pitfalls of the traditional ML framework and explain how it can be improved with human-in-the-loop techniques. Specifically, we applied active learning strategies to the automatic scoring of a story recall task and compared the results to a traditional approach. Results Human-in-the-loop methodologies supplied a greater understanding of where the model was least confident or had knowledge gaps during training. As compared to the traditional framework, less than half of the training data were needed to reach a given accuracy. Conclusions Human-in-the-loop ML is an approach to data collection and model creation that harnesses active learning to select the most critical data needed to increase a model’s accuracy and generalizability more efficiently than classic random sampling would otherwise allow. Such techniques may additionally operate as safeguards from spurious predictions and can aid in decreasing disparities that artificial intelligence systems otherwise propagate.

resources.title: A model for types and levels of human interaction with automation
resources.abstract: Technical developments in computer hardware and software now make it possible to introduce automation into virtually all aspects of human-machine systems. Given these technical capabilities, which system functions should be automated and to what extent? We outline a model for types and levels of automation that provides a framework and an objective basis for making such choices. Appropriate selection is important because automation does not merely supplant but changes human activity and can impose new coordination demands on the human operator. We propose that automation can be applied to four broad classes of functions: 1) information acquisition; 2) information analysis; 3) decision and action selection; and 4) action implementation. Within each of these types, automation can be applied across a continuum of levels from low to high, i.e., from fully manual to fully automatic. A particular system can involve automation of all four types at different levels. The human performance consequences of particular types and levels of automation constitute primary evaluative criteria for automation design using our model. Secondary evaluative criteria include automation reliability and the costs of decision/action consequences, among others. Examples of recommended types and levels of automation are provided to illustrate the application of the model to automation design.

resources.title: Tutorial: Get Started in the Amazon A2I Console
resources.abstract: Tutorial on using the Amazon A2I console to leverage Augmented AI for document review using Amazon Textract or image moderation using Amazon Rekognition.

resources.title: When combinations of humans and AI are useful: A systematic review and meta-analysis
resources.abstract: Inspired by the increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) to augment humans, researchers have studied human–AI systems involving different tasks, systems and populations. Despite such a large body of work, we lack a broad conceptual understanding of when combinations of humans and AI are better than either alone. Here we addressed this question by conducting a preregistered systematic review and meta-analysis of 106 experimental studies reporting 370 effect sizes. We searched an interdisciplinary set of databases (the Association for Computing Machinery Digital Library, the Web of Science and the Association for Information Systems eLibrary) for studies published between 1 January 2020 and 30 June 2023. Each study was required to include an original human-participants experiment that evaluated the performance of humans alone, AI alone and human–AI combinations. First, we found that, on average, human–AI combinations performed significantly worse than the best of humans or AI alone (Hedges’ g = −0.23; 95% confidence interval, −0.39 to −0.07). Second, we found performance losses in tasks that involved making decisions and significantly greater gains in tasks that involved creating content. Finally, when humans outperformed AI alone, we found performance gains in the combination, but when AI outperformed humans alone, we found losses. Limitations of the evidence assessed here include possible publication bias and variations in the study designs analysed. Overall, these findings highlight the heterogeneity of the effects of human–AI collaboration and point to promising avenues for improving human–AI systems.

resources.title: Article 14: Human Oversight | EU Artificial Intelligence Act
Human-in-the-loop machine learning: a state of the art
resources.abstract: Researchers are defining new types of interactions between humans and machine learning algorithms generically called human-in-the-loop machine learning. Depending on who is in control of the learning process, we can identify: active learning, in which the system remains in control; interactive machine learning, in which there is a closer interaction between users and learning systems; and machine teaching, where human domain experts have control over the learning process. Aside from control, humans can also be involved in the learning process in other ways. In curriculum learning human domain experts try to impose some structure on the examples presented to improve the learning; in explainable AI the focus is on the ability of the model to explain to humans why a given solution was chosen. This collaboration between AI models and humans should not be limited only to the learning process; if we go further, we can see other terms that arise such as Usable and Useful AI. In this paper we review the state of the art of the techniques involved in the new forms of relationship between humans and ML algorithms. Our contribution is not merely listing the different approaches, but to provide definitions clarifying confusing, varied and sometimes contradictory terms; to elucidate and determine the boundaries between the different methods; and to correlate all the techniques searching for the connections and influences between them.

sample_claims.text: The autonomous vehicle system requires qualified driver intervention before executing manoeuvres flagged as high-risk by safety criteria
All loan denial decisions that are appealed are reviewed by qualified underwriters, and the applicant receives the underwriter's recorded reasons for the outcome
The diagnostic support system prevents treatment recommendations from being actioned until reviewed by a licensed physician
Every automated rejection in the recruitment pipeline is held until a named reviewer has confirmed or reversed it, and each decision is logged with the reviewer's reason
The content moderation system escalates borderline cases to human moderators based on defined criteria rather than relying solely on automated classification

techniques.name: Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law Risk and Impact Assessment
techniques.description: HUDERIA is the Council of Europe's methodology for identifying and assessing the risks an AI system poses to human rights, democracy and the rule of law, and for planning how to prevent or reduce them, from design through deployment to retirement. It is non-binding guidance that public and private organisations may use or adapt in whole or in part; it was drawn up to support risk assessment in line with the Council of Europe's Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, and the human rights treaties its resources cite are illustrative, binding only the states that are parties to them. A multidisciplinary team first runs a context-based risk analysis (COBRA): it scopes the system's purpose, data and affected groups, works through risk factors in the system's application, design and deployment contexts, maps potential impacts on specific rights and on democratic and legal processes, gives each impact an initial rating, and triages the system, deciding whether further assessment is needed and whether the system should be built or deployed at all. Impacts are rated for severity, judged by scale (how serious the harm is), scope (how many people, which groups and for how long) and reversibility (whether those affected can be restored to their earlier position), and for probability; for systems that may pose significant risks, the team may engage affected stakeholders and then re-examines and re-rates each impact in a fuller risk and impact assessment. The output is a mitigation plan that prefers avoiding a harm to reducing, repairing or compensating for it, names who is responsible for each measure, outlines where appropriate the remedies open to affected people, and schedules repeat reviews as the system and its context change.

example_use_cases.description: A city council's children's services department is offered a model that ranks safeguarding referrals for follow-up. A team of caseworkers, a data scientist and a human rights lawyer runs the context-based risk analysis, maps impacts on family life, non-discrimination and fair procedure, and at triage asks whether existing caseworker screening would serve the problem better and whether the referral data represent the families concerned, before deciding whether to procure the model at all.

A recruitment software company assessing a CV-screening model engages disabled and older job seekers, the groups its analysis found most exposed, then rates each mapped impact for scale, scope, reversibility and probability under a scoring rule it writes down. Its mitigation plan drops a feature that scored video interviews, an 'avoid' measure, rather than relying on correcting decisions afterwards, and names the owner of each remaining measure.

A national tax authority that assessed its fraud-risk model before launch repeats the risk and impact assessment when it adds bank-transaction data, and again when a change in benefit rules alters who is flagged. Each review updates the mitigation plan and the information and appeal routes offered to people wrongly flagged, so the assessment on file describes the system as it now runs.

A health ministry outside Europe adapts HUDERIA for a symptom-checker chatbot, keeping the treaty references in the risk-factor and impact lists only for the instruments its state is party to and adding its own constitution, health law and data protection law, while keeping the four elements and the severity variables so that its assessments follow a published structure others can recognise and check.

limitations.description: HUDERIA leaves the rule for combining scale, scope, reversibility and probability into a risk level, and the thresholds used at triage, to the authorities or project teams applying it. Two teams can rate the same system differently and both be following the methodology, so an assessment can be compared or checked only if the team records the scoring rule it chose and why.

Stakeholder engagement and the detailed risk and impact assessment are optional, and are expected mainly for systems that the team's own triage finds may pose significant risks. A team that under-rates a system at triage can skip the stages most likely to expose the problem, so the evidence is stronger when someone outside the team has reviewed the triage reasoning.

The assessment rests on documents, expert judgement and what stakeholders report; it does not test the system. Probability ratings made before a system is built can be little more than informed estimates, so claims about how the system actually behaves, for example whether it treats groups differently, need test results from other techniques alongside the assessment.

HUDERIA assesses one system at a time. It asks teams to consider cumulative effects when a system runs alongside others serving similar purposes, which is where many harms to democratic and legal processes arise, but gives no method for estimating them. An assessment can therefore find each system acceptable while their combined contribution to a wider harm goes unmeasured, so claims about societal impact need evidence beyond a single assessment.

A full assessment needs people who can judge impacts on rights in law as well as people who understand the system's data and design, and it is meant to be repeated over the system's life. Organisations without access to human rights legal expertise may be unable to carry out the impact mapping and mitigation planning to the depth the methodology intends.

resources.title: HUDERIA Methodology and Model: Methodology for assessing the risks and impacts of artificial intelligence systems from the perspective of human rights, democracy and the rule of law
Human rights, democracy, and the rule of law assurance framework for AI systems: A proposal

sample_claims.text: Before procurement, the safeguarding referral model went through a documented HUDERIA context-based risk analysis, and the triage decision, including whether to adopt the system at all, is recorded with its reasons.

Every impact identified for the CV-screening model was rated for scale, scope, reversibility and probability under a written scoring rule, and each impact rated high has a mitigation measure with a named owner.
Groups identified as most exposed to the system's potential harms were consulted before the risk and impact assessment, and the assessment records which impacts their input added or changed.

The risk and impact assessment of the fraud-risk model has been repeated after each change to its data sources or to the rules it applies, and the mitigation plan and the remedies for people wrongly flagged were updated each time.

techniques.name: SMACTR Internal Algorithmic Audit
techniques.description: SMACTR is an internal audit procedure for AI systems, proposed by Raji and colleagues in 2020, in which an audit team inside the developing organisation but separate from the product team examines a system during development and before launch against the ethical objectives and requirements the organisation has declared for it. The audit runs in five stages, each producing set documents. In Scoping, auditors review the product requirements and the declared objectives and write an ethical review of the use case, drawing in independent domain experts and marginalised groups, and a social impact assessment; in Mapping, they map the people involved, review existing design records, interview the engineers and begin a failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA), a systematic review of the foreseeable ways the system could fail and their effects, used to rank risks for testing. In Artefact Collection, a checklist confirms that the expected development documents, such as model cards and datasheets, exist; in Testing, auditors run tests chosen from the FMEA's priorities, such as adversarial probing with tailored inputs, and rate each risk high, mid or low from its likelihood and severity in an ethical risk analysis chart; in Reflection, they set the results against the declared objectives, finalise the risk analysis and agree a remediation plan with the engineering team. The documents are kept in an algorithmic design history file, from which the auditors write a summary report that leadership can use to decide whether the system launches, changes or is abandoned.

example_use_cases.description: An insurer's internal audit team audits a claims-triage model before launch. Interviews in Mapping reveal that a field used as a proxy for chronic illness was dropped late without the requirements being updated; the FMEA ranks under-prioritising complex claims as the top risk, so Testing concentrates on claims from people with several conditions, and the summary report goes to the risk committee with a remediation plan and a recommendation to delay launch.

A software company's responsible-AI audit team audits a customer-support chatbot. Artefact Collection finds no datasheet for the fine-tuning conversations, so the auditors require the product team to write one before testing; prompts drawn from the FMEA then test whether the bot discloses other customers' account details or gives poorer answers to customers writing in non-standard English, and the ethical risk chart and remediation plan record what must change before release.

A government digital service's audit team, which reports to the agency's chief risk officer rather than to the delivery programme, audits an in-house model that prioritises housing repair requests before it replaces manual triage. The chief risk officer uses the summary report to decide whether the model goes live, and the design history file and report are filed where the agency's external auditors and ombudsman can later inspect them.

limitations.description: The auditors are employees of the organisation they audit and share its interests; the authors acknowledge that independence is hard to keep and that audits risk becoming reputation management. Findings carry more weight when the audit team reports outside the product's management line and the design history file can be examined by an outside party.

The system is judged against the ethical objectives the organisation declares for it, which the authors note have been criticised as vague, and the paper leaves open what level of performance, for example how close to parity across groups, counts as acceptable. A clean audit shows consistency with the standards and thresholds the organisation chose to declare, and says nothing about any external standard it did not adopt.

The Testing stage prescribes no particular tests; the authors expect tests to vary widely by system and to follow the FMEA's priorities. What the audit can show about the system's behaviour therefore depends on the tests the team chooses, and a failure mode the FMEA did not foresee is likely to go untested.

The audit is deliberately slow and document-heavy, and the authors note that fast, iterative development is hard to audit. Its results describe the system at the time of the audit, so a model retrained or reconfigured afterwards is not covered unless the relevant stages are repeated.

The paper does not say which systems should be audited or in how much depth, leaving that to the organisation, and it illustrates the procedure only on two hypothetical client projects. Published evidence of how well it finds problems in real systems is limited.

sample_claims.text: The claims-triage model was audited before launch by a team outside its product line, through all five SMACTR stages, and the audit report and design history file are held where the risk committee can inspect them.
Every risk rated high in the audit's ethical risk analysis chart has a remediation action agreed with the engineering team and recorded as completed, or formally accepted, before release.
The tests run in the audit's Testing stage were selected from the failure modes ranked highest in the FMEA, and each result is traced to the failure mode it tests.
The documentation the audit required, including a datasheet for the chatbot's fine-tuning data and a model card, was complete before testing began, as recorded in the audit checklist.
